top.title: Why some people escape Alzheimer’s despite carrying a high-risk gene
top.summary: Scientists have discovered why some people with a high genetic risk of Alzheimer’s remain mentally sharp into their 80s, uncovering a rare mutation that protects the brain from harmful protein buildup. The findings reveal a potential new way to prevent early brain damage and could pave the way for treatments that mimic this natural defense.
top.text: Some people carry one of the strongest genetic risk factors for Alzheimer's disease yet never develop it, remaining mentally sharp well into their 80s. For years, scientists have wondered what protects these individuals despite their increased genetic vulnerability. Now, researchers at Columbia University have uncovered a biological mechanism that could help explain this remarkable resistance. Their findings point to a rare genetic mutation that protects the brain's blood vessels from damage, potentially opening a new path toward Alzheimer's treatments. The discovery builds on research the team published two years ago involving APOE ε4, a gene variant strongly associated with Alzheimer's risk. The scientists found that some people carrying APOE ε4 also possess a rare protective mutation in the fibronectin (FN1) gene. Fibronectin is a protein that helps support the structure of tissues. However, in people with APOE ε4, excessive amounts can accumulate around blood vessels in the brain, potentially compromising a critical protective system known as the blood-brain barrier. The rare FN1 mutation appears to limit this buildup and the damage associated with it. That earlier discovery suggested an intriguing possibility: What if scientists could develop a treatment that recreates the protection provided by this rare mutation? A new study published in Nature Aging brings that possibility closer by identifying how excess fibronectin damages the brain's protective barrier and revealing potential ways to interrupt the process. "This new study takes us from a genetic clue to a disease mechanism," says Caghan Kizil, the study's corresponding author and professor of neurological sciences in the Department of Neurology and the Taub Institute for Research on Alzheimer's Disease and the Aging Brain at Columbia University Vagelos College of Physicians and Surgeons. "We knew that changes in fibronectin could protect against Alzheimer's, but we didn't know why excess fibronectin was harmful in the first place. This study gives us that detailed mechanism -- and with it, ideas for how to reproduce that natural protection." The blood-brain barrier serves as a protective boundary between the bloodstream and the brain. Made up of tightly connected cells surrounding the brain's blood vessels, it carefully regulates which substances can enter brain tissue while helping maintain conditions necessary for removing potentially harmful waste. When this barrier becomes damaged or excessively permeable, substances that would normally be kept out can enter the brain more easily. Such disruptions may contribute to inflammation and other processes involved in neurological diseases, including Alzheimer's. To investigate the role of fibronectin, the Columbia team combined several advanced research approaches. They examined human brain tissue and cerebrospinal fluid, the clear liquid surrounding the brain and spinal cord, using genetic and epigenetic analyses to explore changes in DNA and gene activity. Their investigation also included single-cell sequencing, which reveals the activity of individual cells, and spatial imaging to examine where biological changes occur within tissues. Additional experiments involved human stem-cell models, three-dimensional cultures of blood vessels, and studies in zebrafish and mice. Despite the variety of methods, the findings consistently pointed to the same mechanism: APOE ε4 promotes the production and accumulation of fibronectin around the brain's blood vessels. In mice engineered to carry human APOE ε4, researchers measured nearly twice as much fibronectin in the brain as in mice carrying APOE ε3, another common version of the gene. The greater accumulation was accompanied by evidence that the blood-brain barrier had become leaky. One experiment provided especially important evidence that fibronectin does more than simply accumulate in damaged blood vessels. The researchers increased human fibronectin specifically in astrocytes, specialized support cells that help maintain the blood-brain barrier and keep the brain functioning properly. Increasing fibronectin in these cells was enough to disrupt the barrier, allowing it to become more permeable. Conversely, reducing fibronectin improved the barrier's ability to function normally. These results provided experimental evidence that excess fibronectin can directly contribute to blood-brain barrier damage rather than merely appearing alongside it. "The animal experiments allowed us to move beyond association," says co-first author Prabesh Bhattarai, an associate research scientist in the Kizil lab. "When we increased fibronectin in astroglia, the barrier became permeable. When we reduced fibronectin, barrier function improved." The team then investigated the molecular events responsible for the damage. They found that excessive fibronectin interferes with communication between cells by activating abnormal signals through integrins, proteins that help cells sense and respond to their surroundings, and an enzyme known as focal adhesion kinase. These abnormal signals disrupt a network of growth factors called VEGF, HBEGF, and IGF1. Although growth factors are often associated with cell development and repair, these particular signaling molecules also help astrocytes and blood vessel cells coordinate their activities to maintain a healthy blood-brain barrier. When their communication becomes disrupted, the barrier can lose its integrity, potentially leaving brain tissue more vulnerable to damage. "Single-cell analysis allowed us to examine this pathway in the different cells that maintain the brain's blood vessels," says co-first author Elanur Yilmaz, an associate research scientist in the Kizil lab. "We observed the same biological pattern across experimental models and human Alzheimer's tissue, making the mechanism especially compelling." Evidence From Human Brains Strengthens the Alzheimer's Connection Importantly, the researchers found signs of similar biological disturbances in human samples, suggesting that the process identified in laboratory experiments may also contribute to Alzheimer's disease in people carrying APOE ε4. Analyses of brain tissue and cerebrospinal fluid showed that elevated fibronectin levels were associated with inflammation in astrocytes. Genetic and gene-regulation analyses also connected FN1 to blood vessel disease and changes involving VEGFA, a growth factor that plays an important role in maintaining healthy brain blood vessels. Together, these findings provide multiple lines of evidence linking excess fibronectin to the vascular damage associated with APOE ε4. "The convergence of these independent human datasets strengthens the case that fibronectin is part of the APOE ε4-related vascular disease process," says Badri Vardarajan, associate professor of neurological science in the Department of Neurology, Gertrude H. Sergievsky Center, and Taub Institute, who collaborated on this discovery of the FN1 mutation. A Rare Genetic Defense Could Inspire New Alzheimer's Treatments The potential implications are significant because APOE ε4 is the strongest common genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's disease. Approximately one in five people carries at least one copy of this gene variant. Although carrying APOE ε4 does not guarantee that someone will develop Alzheimer's, it increases their likelihood of developing the disease. Understanding why certain carriers remain unaffected could reveal new opportunities for prevention and treatment. One strategy would be to prevent harmful amounts of fibronectin from accumulating around the brain's blood vessels. Another would involve blocking the abnormal cellular signals triggered by excess fibronectin. A third possibility would be to restore the growth factor signaling that allows astrocytes and blood vessel cells to maintain the blood-brain barrier. top.title: Something strange is happening beneath a volcano near 2 million people
top.summary: Scientists have discovered evidence of two hidden magma sources beneath Nicaragua’s Masaya volcano, where satellite observations revealed mysterious ground movements suggesting magma is shifting deep underground. The findings could improve eruption forecasting for the active volcano, which sits near 2 million people and attracts tourists to its spectacular lava lake.
top.text: A volcano famous for its glowing lava lake is hiding a surprisingly complex system of magma deep underground. Scientists at Penn State have uncovered evidence of two previously unrecognized magma sources beneath Nicaragua's active Masaya volcano, raising new questions about how molten rock moves beneath the surface. The discovery is particularly important because approximately 2 million people live within 13 miles of the volcano, which is also a popular tourist destination. Understanding its underground activity could help scientists recognize warning signs of future eruptions and better protect nearby communities. Using six years of satellite observations, researchers tracked subtle changes in the ground around Masaya. They discovered that one part of the volcano initially sank before beginning to rise, possibly indicating that fresh magma was entering a deep reservoir. Meanwhile, the ground around its active Santiago crater and lava lake continued to sink, suggesting that a separate, shallower magma reservoir was behaving differently. The findings, published in Geophysical Research Letters , reveal that the volcano's underground magma system may be considerably more complicated than previously understood. "These observations help scientists better understand how magma moves beneath Masaya and may improve monitoring and eruption forecasting in the future," said lead author Lizzie Johnson, who earned her bachelor's degree in geosciences from Penn State in May. Located near Managua, Nicaragua's capital, Masaya is a geologically complex volcano featuring multiple overlapping craters and calderas. Calderas are large depressions that generally form when the ground collapses after magma is removed from an underground chamber. Although scientists have studied Masaya for years, the movement of magma through its underground reservoirs and passageways remains poorly understood. These systems can change over time, making it difficult to determine exactly what is happening beneath the volcano. "Having a thorough understanding of Masaya's volcanic activity and its related hazards is critical as around 2 million people live near Masaya and the caldera is a national park and popular tourist destination," Johnson said. "Although Masaya last produced a major lava flow in 1772, its persistent degassing often produces dangerously high concentrations of sulfur dioxide volcanic gas." Sulfur dioxide is a potentially harmful volcanic gas released as magma approaches or remains near the surface. Even without a major eruption, elevated concentrations can create dangerous conditions for visitors and surrounding communities. Young Cheol Kim, who completed his doctorate in geosciences at Penn State this summer, explained that monitoring the volcano continuously is essential for distinguishing normal activity from changes that might signal increasing volcanic hazards. "Doing continuous monitoring allows us to understand the baseline activity and identify see if things are changing," he said, explaining that certain shifts in volcanic behavior could indicate a period of heightened activity or a possible eruption. "And then if there is a need to warn people, we can do that in a timely manner." To investigate Masaya's underground activity, the researchers analyzed measurements collected by the Sentinel-1 satellite, which observes the volcano approximately once every 12 days. The team used a technique called interferometric synthetic aperture radar (InSAR), which can detect extremely small changes in the elevation of Earth's surface. By comparing satellite measurements taken at different times, scientists can identify areas where the ground is rising or sinking. The technique combines two important capabilities. Synthetic aperture radar sends microwave signals toward Earth's surface, allowing satellites to collect measurements even when clouds obscure the ground. Interferometry compares the returning radar signals to detect changes in distance between the satellite and the surface. This is especially valuable in tropical regions, where frequent cloud cover can make conventional satellite imagery less reliable. "Cloud penetration is important for volcanoes because many of them, like Masaya, are in tropical areas where there is often cloud cover," Kim explained. "And when we look at all the different satellite images across multiple years, we can see how the distance between the satellite and the ground changes, where it is uplifting or subsiding." By examining these subtle movements over time, researchers can investigate processes happening far below the surface without directly observing the magma itself. The satellite measurements revealed an intriguing pattern between 2018 and 2024. During the first part of the study, the ground within Masaya's caldera gradually subsided, meaning it moved downward. Later, the same general area began to rise. Scientists believe this transition could reflect changes in the amount of magma stored underground. When magma drains away from a reservoir, the overlying ground can sink. When additional magma enters and increases pressure within a reservoir, the surface may rise. The most surprising finding was that the area surrounding Santiago crater did not follow the same pattern. Instead, it continued to sink throughout the six-year study, even as the broader caldera began rising. "When it's subsiding, that means that there's probably magma draining away from the volcano, but once the ground starts uplifting again, that can mean that there's potentially new magma moving in," Johnson said. "At the same time, the area directly around the active Santiago crater deflated over the entire study period independently of the transition to inflation of the main reservoir. This indicates that the plumbing system is more complex and could be due to decreasing magma in a second, shallower reservoir." Together, these observations suggest that Masaya may have at least two distinct parts of its magma storage system undergoing different changes. A deeper source could be supplying additional magma to the main reservoir, while a shallower reservoir near Santiago crater may be losing magma. This would help explain why different sections of the same volcano moved in opposite directions. Understanding these underground movements is important because changes in the ground can provide clues about where magma is accumulating, where it is moving, and how it might eventually reach the surface. The researchers emphasized that their observations did not reveal any immediate danger to communities surrounding Masaya. However, identifying the volcano's normal behavior and understanding its magma supply system could make it easier to recognize unusual changes in the future. Continued satellite observations, combined with more detailed computer models, could also help scientists better understand the connections between underground magma reservoirs and volcanic activity at the surface. "Further long-term geodetic and modeling studies will provide a more thorough understanding and allow for effective hazard monitoring and mitigation at Masaya and other lava-lake hosting basaltic volcanoes," Johnson said. The findings may therefore have implications beyond Nicaragua, particularly for other active volcanoes that contain persistent lava lakes and complex underground magma systems. She completed the research as part of her Schreyer's Honors College thesis, working alongside graduate researchers, including Kim, to analyze satellite measurements and develop her scientific skills. top.title: Physicists create a bizarre new quantum state called a fractional fermi sea
top.summary: Physicists have discovered a strange new state of quantum matter in which ultracold atoms defy familiar organizational rules, forming a highly excited yet surprisingly orderly configuration called a "fractional Fermi sea." The discovery challenges established quantum theories and hints at exotic quasiparticles that scientists have dubbed potential "super-Fermions."
top.text: Physicists have uncovered a strange new form of quantum behavior in which particles organize themselves in ways that challenge established theories. Even more surprising, the particles maintain a remarkable hidden order despite being driven into an extremely energetic state. In a study published in Physical Review Letters , researchers from the group led by Hanns-Christoph Nägerl, working with theoretical physicist Alvise Bastianello of the CNRS and Université Paris-Dauphine, describe how to engineer an exotic quantum state known as a "fractional Fermi sea." The breakthrough involves pushing ultracold cesium atoms far beyond their normal conditions by repeatedly changing how strongly they attract or repel one another. Rather than simply becoming disordered, the particles rearrange themselves into an unusual configuration that behaves differently from the quantum systems scientists have traditionally studied. The theoretical findings provide the foundation for recent experimental research conducted by Nägerl's team at the Department of Experimental Physics. Under ordinary conditions, quantum particles follow well-established rules that determine how they arrange themselves, particularly at extremely low temperatures. One important example involves fermions, a category of particles that includes electrons. These particles cannot all occupy the same quantum state, so they fill available energy levels according to specific restrictions. At very low temperatures, this arrangement produces what physicists call a Fermi sea. But what happens when researchers deliberately disrupt the conditions that normally govern how particles behave? As Alvise Bastianello explains: "Fermions, for instance, stack neatly into the available energy states to form the so-called 'Fermi sea'. But what happens if one forces interacting atoms to continuously cycle through extreme conditions, smoothly shifting them from strongly repelling each other to strongly attracting each other?" To investigate this possibility, the researchers studied ultracold cesium atoms confined to a one-dimensional system. This means the atoms are restricted to moving along a single direction, creating an environment in which their quantum interactions can be studied with exceptional control. The team examined what happens when the interactions between these atoms are repeatedly adjusted, cycling between powerful repulsion and attraction. Their calculations revealed something unexpected. Starting from the ground state, the lowest energy configuration available to the system, the atoms could be driven into a highly excited state without losing their underlying organization. The researchers call this unusual arrangement a fractional Fermi sea because its particles appear to obey a modified rule governing how quantum states are occupied. "Instead of simply heating the system, the interaction cycle reorganizes the atoms into a new many-body state," says Yi Zeng, the leading author of this study. "This gives us a controlled way to explore quantum matter beyond the usual equilibrium paradigms." One of the most intriguing features of the fractional Fermi sea is that its particles remain organized even though the system has been pushed far from equilibrium. In physics, equilibrium describes a condition in which a system's overall properties have settled into a stable balance. Systems driven far from equilibrium can behave in complicated and unexpected ways, making them particularly challenging to understand. Yet the fractional Fermi sea is not simply a collection of excited particles behaving randomly. Instead, it contains distinctive mathematical patterns that reveal a deeper structure. Among these patterns are pronounced ripples called Friedel oscillations. These are wave-like variations associated with the way quantum particles influence one another. The researchers also identified unusual patterns in how correlations between particles weaken with increasing distance, even when the repulsive interactions are relatively weak. These signatures are important because they differ from predictions associated with Tomonaga-Luttinger liquid theory, a long-established framework for describing how interacting quantum particles behave in one-dimensional systems. The findings therefore point toward a previously unexplored type of quantum behavior that cannot be fully described using this familiar theoretical picture. "This state is highly excited, but it is not random," says Hanns-Christoph Nägerl, the group leader. "It has a hidden order that becomes visible in its correlations." The strange behavior also raises questions about the effective particles that emerge within the system. Physicists call these collective excitations quasiparticles because they can behave like individual particles even though they arise from the coordinated motion of many interacting particles. Nägerl suggests that the unusual excitations might eventually deserve a name of their own. "We are not yet sure how we should name these new quasiparticles. Perhaps 'super-Fermions'?" The discovery suggests that fractional Fermi seas represent an exotic critical phase of quantum matter, with characteristic patterns of particle correlations that extend beyond existing descriptions of one-dimensional quantum systems. It also demonstrates the growing power of quantum simulation, a technique that allows scientists to use carefully controlled quantum systems to investigate physical behavior that would otherwise be difficult to reproduce or study. Ultracold atoms are particularly useful for this purpose because researchers can precisely adjust their interactions and observe how the resulting quantum states change. Rather than limiting these experiments to recreating phenomena already understood through established theories, scientists can now explore deliberately engineered states that reveal entirely new possibilities. As Hanns-Christoph Nägerl says: "The discovery of fractional Fermi seas shows how far we can push quantum simulation: not only reproducing known models, but creating and probing states that go beyond established paradigms." The current publication establishes the theoretical framework for fractional Fermi seas. A companion study describing their experimental realization through quantum simulation is undergoing peer review. Together, the research points toward new ways of investigating the fundamental behavior of quantum matter, including unusual collective excitations and hidden forms of order that emerge only when particles are pushed far outside their normal conditions. top.title: Your brain maps out numbers, including integers and fractions
top.summary: From learning to count to solving complex calculations, math requires an inherent organization of information. A team of researchers led by Stanislas Dehaene, Ph.D., and Daniela Valério, Ph.D., at the INSERM-CEA Cognitive Neuroimaging Unit (Unicog) Lab in France took dynamic brain scans of adults presented with fractions and integers. Their findings, published on Oct. 22 in the journal PLOS Biology, revealed a map of brain activity that underlies how we arrange numerical information.

top.summary: Admission to a pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) can have lasting psychological effects on both children receiving treatment and their parents. To investigate the effects of psychosocial interventions on parents' emotional health, researchers searched five major academic databases for studies published through January 2026 and analyzed eight randomized controlled trials evaluating psychosocial interventions in parents of children admitted to the PICU. The interventions included visits to follow-up clinics, psychological screening with referral, telephone-based psychoeducation, palliative care consultations and acceptance and commitment therapy delivered via videoconference. top.title: Gut microbiome may help explain why sleep improvement varies after hydrogen supplementation
top.summary: A Hiroshima University–led clinical trial found that hydrogen supplementation did not significantly improve sleep quality compared with a placebo; however, exploratory analyses suggest that differences in the abundance of hydrogen-producing gut bacteria may be associated with individual differences in sleep-related responses.

top.title: Plant-first food pyramid brings international dietary guidelines together in adaptable global guide
top.summary: Dietary guidance varies by country, and no international food pyramid has brought its recommendations together until now. BYU nutritional science professor Karen Della Corte led a global team of nutrition scientists to develop an International Food Guide Pyramid that reflects broad scientific agreement and can be adapted across cultures and borders.

top.title: Power cuts and sleep: Students link load shedding to anxiety, disrupted rest and lower grades
top.summary: South Africa endured its worst year of load shedding (scheduled power cuts by the country's utility, Eskom) in 2023. The power went off on 335 of the year's 365 days, often several times a day. Since then, the country has gone more than a year and a half without these planned power cuts.

top.title: Elections are more predictable than they look
top.summary: As politics in America become more polarized and each voting cycle seems more fraught than the last, a common narrative in the media is that each election is unique and increasingly unpredictable. But new research shows that congressional elections follow strong statistical patterns, even when individual races produce surprises.

top.title: Potatoes could be the secret to better plant-based meat, say food scientists
top.summary: Potatoes could hold the key to making better gluten-free plant-based meat, according to a new study.

top.title: Tegoprubart preserves kidney function better than tacrolimus in first-time transplant patients, trial suggests
top.summary: The phase 2 BESTOW clinical trial showed that tegoprubart (a novel anti-CD40L antibody therapy) was better at preserving kidney function than tacrolimus (the current standard of care) in immunosuppressive regimens in adults receiving their first kidney transplant. Kidney graft function stabilized after the first month of treatment and remained higher in tegoprubart-treated patients than in tacrolimus-treated patients at each reported time point, with a statistically significant kidney function benefit at 18 months. top.title: ESMO: New analysis reinforces survival benefits of targeted therapy for advanced pancreatic cancer
top.summary: A new analysis of a phase 3 clinical trial found that the targeted drug daraxonrasib improved survival compared with standard chemotherapy across multiple groups of patients with advanced pancreatic cancer, including those with different RAS mutations and those without an identified RAS mutation.

top.title: Postpartum recovery window may play a critical role in maternal aging and long-term health
top.summary: In many studies, it appears that women who have more children have a higher risk of heart disease and a shorter life span, but this effect is inconsistent across populations and no good explanation for it exists. Against this backdrop, new tools to assess biological age—the age reflected by one's biological state, rather than simply the number of years they have been alive—have revealed that pregnancy temporarily elevates biological age, while postpartum recovery can return it closer to baseline.

top.title: Are 'mega-Earths' real? Stellar activity may explain these oversized rocky worlds
top.summary: A new study suggests that some of the heaviest rocky planets ever reported may not be as heavy as they look. These so-called 'mega-Earths,' rocky planets weighing more than about 10 Earths, could be an illusion created by activity on their host stars. The paper was posted to the arXiv preprint server on Oct. 8.

top.title: Paying for the past: Norway's finder's fees favor gold's weight over what it tells us
top.summary: Ten years ago, in 2016, a metal detectorist came upon a hoard of gold. It had been buried in the dirt for around 1,800 years and consisted of around 396 grams (14 ounces) of gold rings. The detectorist handed in his finds to a museum and received the largest finder's fee ever paid out in Norwegian history. He had been rewarded for the gold weight, not its rarity.

top.title: Parental benefit encouraged people to have children in Estonia, but fathers mainly applied for financial reasons
top.summary: A generous parental leave reform was introduced in Estonia in 2004. This increased the likelihood of a second or third child being born into the family and also shortened the interval between births, according to Sanan Abdullayev's doctoral thesis, defended at Tallinn University. At the same time, taking shared parental leave did not necessarily mean that the father took time off work and assumed primary responsibility for the children while receiving the benefit.

top.title: Baby manta rays hunker down close to coasts before facing the open ocean's dangers
top.summary: Giant manta rays can grow up to nine meters (30 feet) long with a disk size of seven meters (23 feet) across and weigh up to 2,000 kg (4,400 pounds). This size leaves them with very few natural enemies once they reach adulthood at around eight to 10 years old. But giant manta ray babies, called pups, cannot rely on their size to protect them from predators that live in the open ocean, including several species of shark and orcas.

top.title: Clinical trials generate promising results for improving kidney health
top.summary: The results of numerous high-impact Phase III clinical trials that could affect kidney-related medical care were presented in person at American Society of Nephrology Kidney Week 2026, Oct. 22–25.

top.title: Certain children are more prone to serious eating problems in later life
top.summary: Emotional overeating, sometimes called "comfort eating," is not just an innocent habit.

top.title: Study finds 1 in 5 young adults in the U.S. experience daily anxiety
top.summary: Nearly one in five young adults in the United States reported feeling anxious every day in 2024, up from 15% in 2020. Over the same period, the odds of receiving an anxiety diagnosis as well as use of prescription anxiety medication each rose by roughly a third.

top.title: AAO: Sequential nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy occurs earlier with GLP-1 receptor agonist exposure
top.summary: For patients with nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION), glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist exposure is associated with earlier sequential NAION, according to a study presented at the annual meeting of the American Academy of Ophthalmology, held Oct. 9 to 12 in New Orleans.

top.title: AI identifies tumor aging patterns to predict immunotherapy response across multiple cancer types
top.summary: Even when given the same drug, some patients respond well while others show little or no response. This is particularly true of immunotherapy. A research team at POSTECH (Pohang University of Science and Technology) has developed an artificial intelligence (AI) technology that can predict, in advance, which patients are likely to benefit from treatment.

top.title: Who should have a say in which species are saved? The California condor offers lessons for a global biodiversity treaty
top.summary: In 1987, biologists captured the last free-flying condor to transfer it to captivity, and the largest flying North American bird species was officially declared extinct in the wild. top.text: In 1987, biologists captured the last free-flying condor to transfer it to captivity, and the largest flying North American bird species was officially declared extinct in the wild. Today, after decades of coordinated efforts and millions of dollars spent on captive breeding and reintroduction efforts, more than 300 condors have been restored to their natural environment. It was a victory for the species’ survival, yet this triumph was contested at nearly every step of the way. Conservationists fought bitterly over whether trapping every bird should be considered rescue or surrender. Critics argued that the cost was better spent on other threatened species. Rural communities in Utah and Arizona raised concerns about federal land-use restrictions . Hunting groups such as the National Rifle Association opposed bans on lead ammunition, a leading cause of condor deaths . The condor’s comeback illustrates several questions that governments and conservation organizations grapple with today, including which species get funded and who bears the costs. These are some of the questions being discussed at the U.N. Convention on Biological Diversity conference , being held Oct. 19-30, 2026, in Yerevan, Armenia. In 2022, countries worldwide adopted an agreement at that year’s biodiversity conference to halt and reverse biodiversity loss, known as the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework . It includes goals to raise US$200 billion a year from public and private sources around the world by 2030 to conserve and manage at least 30% of the world’s land, coastal areas and oceans, stop human-caused extinctions and help struggling species survive. The agreement itself doesn’t choose which species to save, but its rules are designed to shape national conservation priorities and guide the funds that pay for conservation. Saving a species like the condor affects local communities and businesses whose activities have put those species at risk. Without local buy-in, pouring money into recovery efforts can fail, yet local communities are often left out of the discussions. An estimated 1 million species are currently threatened with extinction worldwide, and early assessments suggest the world is falling short on most of the agreement’s global biodiversity targets . Because resources are limited, conservationists must weigh trade-offs in deciding which species to protect and how. Should they fund expensive rescue efforts for a species close to extinction, or interventions likely to help multiple species at once? Or maybe they should protect organisms that are unique to a specific geographic region or a species that sustains local livelihoods. Some species are valued for what they do for humanity, such as pollinating crops or purifying water, known as ecosystem services . Honeybees, for example, pollinate over $15 billion worth of crops in the U.S. alone each year. Others hold cultural and spiritual significance, as the condor does for the Yurok Tribe in California. Many conservationists argue that living species possess an inherent right to exist independent of their usefulness to human beings. Getting support for measures to save charismatic species can be easier than for others, however. Think of Greenpeace’s “save the whales” campaign or the World Wildlife Fund’s panda logo. A panda’s adorable face can help pay for its protection and potentially the protection of its surrounding habitat , helping other species living there. A 2025 study examined more than 14,000 species-focused conservation projects from 1992 to 2016. Five mammal groups – primates, carnivores, whales, elephants and rhinos – received 86% of available funding , despite accounting for only one-third of threatened mammal projects. Plants and invertebrates, which are crucial for pollination, nutrient cycling and sustaining food webs, received only 6.6% of the financial backing. Conservation groups and economists at the Paulson Institute estimate that the world needs to spend an additional $1.3 trillion annually on biodiversity conservation and restoration to stop and reverse biodiversity loss. At the 2026 biodiversity conference, delegates will also take up another question that can make or break species recovery: When conservation affects local people, who pays and who gets a say? While conservationists celebrated efforts to return wolves to Europe over the past two decades, some farmers lost livestock to these predators and faced higher costs to protect their flocks. Current European Union funding programs help support livestock protection , but farmers’ ability to shape wolf recovery is part of the story too. Conservation can go terribly wrong if local communities aren’t consulted during planning. In the Ngorongoro Conservation Area, a protected area in Tanzania, the Maasai have fought for years against government orders that they leave the land they have lived on for generations in the name of lion conservation. In March 2026, two presidential commissions recommended that the evictions continue in order to protect wildlife, in a process that included few Maasai , Indigenous peoples’ advocates at the Oakland Institute reported. Protecting vulnerable species often means also supporting the communities living alongside them. At the last round of biodiversity talks in 2024, countries created a permanent advisory body to bring Indigenous peoples and local communities’ knowledge and decisions into the treaty’s decisions. At this year’s conference, known as COP17, they must agree on how that advisory body will operate, including whether these communities get a formal role in decision-making. They are also expected to adopt guidelines for how the 30% global conservation targets apply in Indigenous territories. The international agreement can’t dictate what happens on the ground, but its rules shape national conservation priorities and guide the funds that pay for conservation. That is why the debate over local consultation is at the heart of the 2026 talks. Conservation that is designed for people, rather than with them, risks losing the trust and local cooperation that makes recovery last. Two key issues at the conference involve guaranteeing that Indigenous peoples and local communities have a say in decisions on their territory, including how conservation programs are designed and how resources are allocated. The global biodiversity framework calls for a “ whole-of-society” approach , recognizing that protecting nature needs more than government action alone. But participation is not the same as decision-making power. Advocates for Indigenous groups say communities are too often consulted after priorities are set, rather than being involved in setting them. Whether the farmer paying for fencing or the Indigenous community with connections to a species helps set priorities or is only asked for input after the project has been approved shows whether consultation is genuine or not. The condor’s return shows that nearly extinct species can recover with help. But sustaining a species’ recovery requires protecting the conditions – and supporting the people – that make their survival possible. Researcher Garrett Ordonez, an environmental studies and international relations student at USC, contributed to this article.

top.title: NASA’s Mars orbiter fleet is getting old – here’s how that could affect future exploration
top.summary: NASA lost contact with its Maven spacecraft – the youngest of its Mars orbiters – at the end of 2025. The others in its fleet are over two decades old.
top.text: Currently, about 16,000 satellites are orbiting Earth , providing everything from GPS service and weather reports to phone service in remote locations to people across the globe. In contrast, the highest-ever number of active satellites in orbit around Mars , one of the best-explored other planets in our solar system, is eight. Starting in 2021, there were three from NASA, two from the European Space Agency and one each from the Indian Space Research Organization, the UAE Space Agency and the China National Space Administration. The oldest of these is still 2001 Mars Odyssey, which has now spent 25 years in space, with Mars Express, at 23 years, and the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, at 20 years, hot on its heels. But in December 2025, NASA lost contact with its Maven spacecraft , bringing the total number of active satellites down to seven, and NASA’s to two. The cause of the loss of Maven has still not been publicly released, and NASA officially declared the mission over in June 2026. A final report on the cause of the loss is due later this year. NASA is exploring potential commercial solutions to supplement the current fleet of Mars orbiters. In September 2026, NASA selected Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin to provide a Mars telecommunication satellite no later than Dec. 31, 2028. These satellites are important because future missions will rely on them to communicate with Earth and select safe landing sites on Mars. Planetary scientists like me rely on the data they’ve taken over the past few decades to learn more about our close, red neighbor. The Mars Atmosphere and Volatile EvolutioN, or Maven, spacecraft arrived at Mars in 2014, making it NASA’s youngest orbiter. It was only briefly the youngest in the international Mars family, as the Indian space agency’s Mars Orbiting Mission spacecraft arrived a few days later. The longer any satellite spends in space, the greater the toll of the harsh environment – from extreme temperature swings to solar radiation . Maven, however, appeared generally healthy until it missed a radio check-in – a sign of trouble – after emerging back from behind the planet. Whatever happened to Maven last December was only the second time in the 21st century that NASA had lost contact with an orbiter during otherwise ordinary operations. The other time was in 2006, with Mars Global Surveyor , which NASA ultimately lost, likely due to issues with uploaded software commands. The Mars exploration community, myself among them, is waiting with bated breath to understand why one-third of NASA’s Mars fleet lost contact seemingly overnight. The loss ends a stellar, almost two-decade-long track record of missions ending when expected, not before. Mars science has been in a golden age since 2001 Mars Odyssey arrived at the red planet 25 years ago. NASA has had a Mars rover of some type operating on the surface continuously since 2004 with the Exploration rover landings , so there have been only a handful of years in the 21st century where scientists couldn’t access nearly simultaneous views of Mars from the surface and from orbit. This access gives Mars scientists the ability to study how both the surface and atmosphere change over time. In particular, we can follow changes with Mars’ seasons , which drive about a quarter of its atmosphere onto its surface as seasonal ice . And we have found laundry lists of these changing features, including “spiderlike” araneiform features in the soil that likely develop from carbon dioxide geysers. Learning about rare events like global dust storms , which obscure Mars’ entire surface, also opens up many new questions. We still don’t know what triggers the start of a global dust storm, and they only occur every several Mars years. In Maven’s 11 years at Mars, it was only able to observe one global dust storm, in 2018 . From a practical standpoint, Mars orbiters have their own science missions. However, their powerful radios are also critical for delivering data from landers and rovers , like Perseverance or Curiosity, back to Earth. In the past, NASA has adjusted the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter and Maven orbits to support landings and surface operations. HiRISE (High-Resolution Imaging Science Experiment) aboard the Reconnaissance orbiter, is the highest-resolution camera in orbit to date. Engineers have used data from HiRISE to ensure they could deliver the Mars rovers Curiosity and Perseverance to the surface, as well as the InSight lander . While Mars orbiters and their instrument suites are selected for their science value, they have come to participate in infrastructure that is essential for getting all the possible data back to Earth. These tasks, which go beyond science data collection, make the orbiter fleet critical to Mars exploration. The Dec. 31, 2028, delivery date for the Blue Origin telecommunications Mars orbiter to NASA represents the earliest a new orbiter could be launched for Mars. Mars launch opportunities happen at an approximately 2-year cadence, when Mars and Earth get closest to each other in their respective orbits. During this window, less fuel is needed for the journey. If a new Mars orbiter for science or telecommunications is not launched by the 2028 window, the next opportunity would be in 2030 or 2031. While the Blue Origin telecommunications orbiter would support future exploration missions, the announcement did not outline plans for any science instrumentation onboard. Mars Odyssey will be around 30 years old by then, and the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter around 25. NASA hardware tends to be hardy, often greatly exceeding expectations. For example, the Mars Exploration rovers were meant to last for 90 days, with Spirit ending its mission after over six years and Opportunity after over 14 years. However, orbiters may slowly lose capability over time – the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter’s spectrometer instrument ceased operations in 2023 , while its other instruments are still active. But three or four decades in a space environment is a long tour of duty for any hardware in space, let alone hardware that is pulling double-duty as scientist and radio broadcaster. Much like driving your first car for far longer than you had planned on, the NASA orbiter fleet is waiting to see if the next repair bill means it’s time for an upgrade, or if it’ll have to catch rides from its friends. Until NASA releases its report, scientists and engineers will be waiting to understand what happened to end the Maven spacecraft’s mission early, and how those details can help them keep the current fleet flying until reinforcements finally arrive.

top.title: There should be black holes in our neighborhood. Can we find them?
top.summary: Scientific estimates show that there should be between about 100 million and 1 billion stellar-mass black holes in the Milky Way. But they aren't easy to locate. They're not like supermassive black holes (SMBH) at the centers of galaxies. Those are usually easy to spot for different reasons.

top.title: Canine cancer patients contribute to next-generation minimally invasive cancer therapies for dogs and humans
top.summary: Natural disasters. Hikes. Long, dark nights alone. For many people, dogs offer a sense of safety and comfort in challenging or uncertain times. Cancer researchers at a new lab at Purdue University are partnering with dogs to make cancer less frightening—and less deadly—to some of humanity's very best friends using a technique called tumor ablation.

top.title: Pedal to the metal: NASA's Psyche heads toward asteroid belt
top.summary: With a successful Mars gravity assist in its rearview mirror, NASA's Psyche spacecraft has fired up its thrusters and is accelerating toward the metal-rich asteroid of the same name. During the first leg of its journey, following an October 2023 launch, the mission used its electric propulsion system intermittently to maneuver into the right position to harness Mars' gravity for a propellant-saving speed boost and a slight trajectory change.

top.title: Sinking Antarctic ice reveals a hidden lake's massive water loss
top.summary: The Kronshtadskiy subglacial lake near East Antarctica's Amery Ice Shelf was hidden beneath Antarctica's ice, but its drainage left a mark visible from space as a broad depression that deepened by more than 6 meters (20 feet) at its center.

top.title: El Niño then and now
top.summary: El Niño is part of a natural climate pattern that occurs roughly every two to seven years, bringing warmer-than-normal water to parts of the equatorial Pacific. The most recent very strong El Niño events, in 1997–98 and 2015–16, upended weather patterns. Impacts spanned the planet, from fires in Indonesia and the Amazon to crop failures due to drought in southern Africa to heavy rain and coastal flooding in Southern California. The current El Niño rivals these past heavyweights.

top.title: I’m a Philly forensic psychologist who has conducted dozens of psychopathic evaluations – here’s why an evaluation of R.C. Horsch in the ‘80s didn’t identify him as a possible psychopath
top.summary: Philadelphia police and FBI are conducting a massive investigation into the home where the late R.C. Horsch and his son lived, along with several women who’ve gone missing.
top.text: Seven missing women have been linked to the house that was shared by 44-year-old Eugene Horsch and his late father, Raymond “R.C.” Horsch, in the Olney section of Philadelphia. With five of the seven women feared dead, Philadelphia police and the FBI are conducting a massive investigation of the home . Law enforcement has said Raymond Horsch, who died in 2025 at the age of 82, is the suspected killer . Eugene Horsch has not been charged with any homicides or missing-person offenses related to the missing women. The Horsch house investigation raises questions about serial killers and whether mental health professionals can identify a person at risk of becoming one. The early identification of psychopathy can potentially prevent an escalation of antisocial behavior . As a forensic psychologist , I conduct psychological evaluations to help courts make decisions when someone’s mental health is relevant. I’ve conducted hundreds of forensic psychological evaluations, including dozens with individuals with psychopathic characteristics. I’m not surprised that a previous psychological evaluation of R.C. Horsch, done in the mid-1980s, did not identify him as a potential psychopath. That’s because reliable tools for identifying psychopathy were not available at that time. Psychopathic personality disorder, or psychopathy , is not an officially recognized disorder in the current version of the American Psychiatric Association’s Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders , or DSM. This is the primary diagnostic resource used by mental health professionals in the United States. Although a version of psychopathy was included in prior editions of the DSM, more recent editions have eliminated the diagnosis. This is because of the difficulty in assessing some of the emotional characteristics of psychopathy. Instead, the DSM includes a diagnosis for antisocial personality disorder , which focuses primarily on the behavioral aspects of psychopathy. Psychopathy is generally considered to be a more extreme variant of antisocial personality disorder. While psychopathy is no longer in the DSM, it has been vigorously researched and written about for decades. It is characterized by a distinct group of personality, behavioral and emotional traits. It has been defined in slightly different ways over the years, but some of the traits commonly associated with psychopathy include pathological lying, extreme narcissism, shallow affect, impulsivity and lack of empathy and remorse. Psychopathy is also characterized by a persistent pattern of antisocial or manipulative behaviors. These can range from infidelity and intimidation to aggression and extreme violence. The link between serial killers – individuals who kill several people in separate, unrelated events over a period of time – and psychopathy is not new. Several well-known American serial killers, including Ted Bundy and Jeffrey Dahmer , are suspected to have had psychopathic personality disorder . To be clear, most individuals with psychopathic personality disorder are not serial killers. In fact, people with psychopathic characteristics can be found among corporate executives , elected officials and attorneys . But some traits associated with extreme psychopathy, including the ability to engage in violent behavior with little remorse or guilt, are typically found among serial killers. Given that psychopathic characteristics are common among serial killers, one might wonder: Can mental health professionals identify psychopathy when conducting a psychological evaluation and possibly thwart a future serial killer? Mental health professionals are frequently asked to conduct evaluations of people involved in the criminal justice system who’ve been accused or convicted of serious crimes. For example, we might evaluate someone to help a court determine whether the person is competent to stand trial, or whether they should be found not guilty by reason of insanity. Identifying whether a person has psychopathic characteristics may also be relevant to how a court sentences them after conviction. Individuals with more psychopathic characteristics typically present a higher risk for future criminal behavior . As such, because of the discretion given to judges and juries when it comes to sentencing in most states, courts are more likely to give a longer sentence because of the increased risk to public safety. One of the most widely used psychopathy assessment tools, the psychopathy checklist-revised , or PCL-R, has been the subject of tremendous research over the past few decades. Most studies find that the PCL-R can reliably identify psychopathic characteristics in both research and clinical settings. Individuals with higher PCL-R scores are more psychopathic and, therefore, at higher risk of engaging in future criminal behavior . In 1985, R.C. Horsch was convicted in federal court of charges related to counterfeiting and methamphetamine manufacturing. As part of the federal sentencing proceedings, he underwent a lengthy psychological evaluation, which the Philadelphia Inquirer obtained through a federal records request. The psychologist described Horsch as “ grandiose, mistrustful, suspicious and excessively controlling ,” and noted that he was “consumed by anger.” He concluded that Horsch likely had bipolar disorder and paranoid personality disorder. The psychological evaluation found that Horsch had several characteristics associated with psychopathy, but he was not identified as psychopathic. Why? One answer is that the tests used to identify psychopathic characteristics had not yet been developed in 1985. Although a precursor to the PCL-R was developed in 1980, it was not commercially available, and the PCL-R was not commercially released until 1991. Other psychopathy assessment tests were not developed until after the PCL-R. An astonishing level of research regarding psychopathy has been conducted since the early 1990s. Some research has found that the introduction of psychopathy evidence in both American and Canadian courts has increased dramatically over the past few decades. In these cases, psychopathy evidence is primarily used by the prosecution to argue for a more severe punishment of a convicted defendant. There is also evidence that psychopathy evidence is being inappropriately relied on in death penalty cases . The PCL-R has not been proven to predict violence among inmates on death row or in highly restrictive prison settings. However, it can reliably predict violence among inmates in less secure correctional settings and among individuals about to be released from incarceration. Other research has focused on the brain structure and function associated with psychopathy. Studies have found that the brain region associated with thrill-seeking and impulsive behavior is larger among people with psychopathic characteristics, while regions associated with emotional regulation and fear processing are smaller . Identifying psychopathic characteristics before someone engages in violence is the ideal. However, most psychological evaluations of people involved in the criminal justice system take place only after the person has been arrested or convicted. But if a psychological evaluation is conducted after an individual has been arrested for or convicted of a less serious crime, or when someone is showing early signs of antisocial behavior, the identification of psychopathic characteristics could help courts and treatment providers intervene before there is an escalation to violence.
